title: Energy in a Capacitor: Why It's One Half C V Squared
topic: Energy stored in a capacitor — pushing charge against a rising voltage; the work integral ∫V dq from 0 to Q traces a triangle of area ½QV, giving the three equivalent forms ½CV², ½QV and Q²/(2C)

beats.narration: You push charge onto a capacitor — where does the energy actually go?

elements.content: Charge a capacitor — where does the energy go?

beats.narration: Adding charge raises the voltage. The next little bit of charge has to be pushed against an already higher voltage — so the work piles up.

elements.content: Capacitor symbol — two horizontal plates with a small gap
Charge dots accumulating on top + bottom plates as time advances
V across plates — a value that rises with q
more charge → more voltage → harder to push the next charge

beats.narration: Plot voltage against charge — a straight line from zero up to V. The total work is the area under that line, a triangle with area one half Q V.

elements.content: Horizontal axis: q from 0 to Q; vertical axis: V from 0 to V_final
Straight line V = q/C from origin to (Q, V)
Triangle area filling beneath the line as q advances 0 → Q
Moving (q, V) point sliding up the line
the area under V(q) is the energy stored

beats.narration: Substitute Q equals C V and you get one half C V squared. Substitute V equals Q over C and you get Q squared over two C. Same energy, three shapes.

elements.content: use whichever two quantities you know

beats.narration: The energy lives in the electric field between the plates — it stays there until something gives it somewhere to go.

elements.content: Energy lives in the field between the plates.
(release it through a load and it powers a current)
